title: Least Eligible Bachelor
description: A marriage comedy that understands family pressure better than it develops its romance.
review: Teja has a familiar problem. His family thinks marriage will solve his life, while he is still trying to figure out what kind of life he wants. That is a better starting point than the usual bachelor comedy because the pressure is recognizable.

Harsha Chemudu is suited to a man who is always slightly behind the situation. His awkwardness gives the jokes some personality. Hyper Aadi and the supporting cast bring energy, although the comedy sometimes depends too much on familiar reactions.
The office setting and Madhu's independent plans offer the possibility of a more interesting relationship. Marriage should not simply become a prize Teja receives after enough misunderstandings.

Six episodes give the characters time to change. The problem is that the later portions appear more interested in extending situations than developing the couple. A shorter, sharper season could have made the emotional payoff stronger.

There is enough light comedy to make this an easy casual watch. But the writing needed to ask one more question: does Teja actually understand Madhu, or does he just want his search for a bride to end?
works: Harsha Chemudu's awkward comedy, recognizable family pressure and a promising workplace-romance setup.
misses: Uneven relationship development, familiar jokes and a stretched later portion.

title: Eyes
description: A surveillance thriller that turns watching someone into a disturbing question of power.
review: Eyes begins with a modern fear: somebody can know too much about your life without ever standing near you. The series uses surveillance and stalking to explore how control can disguise itself as concern.

Manu Ashokan takes a premise that could easily become unbelievable and treats it seriously. That confidence is important. A thriller does not need every invention to exist in real life, but it does need consistent consequences.

The ensemble, including Nikhila Vimal, Kani Kusruti and Jaffer Idukki, gives the story several human points of entry. The threat feels more disturbing when the characters have ordinary lives worth protecting.
What makes the central idea interesting is its connection to relationships. A person who constantly checks where somebody goes may call it love. The person being watched may experience it as fear.

The technological mechanism requires some suspension of disbelief, and the heightened twists may not satisfy viewers looking for a strictly realistic investigation. But the underlying subject gives the suspense a sharper edge.
Eyes is most compelling when it remembers that privacy is not merely a technical setting. It is the freedom to live without another person's permission.
works: Tense direction, committed performances, a distinctive surveillance premise and relevant themes.
misses: Far-fetched technology and occasional dependence on heightened thriller logic.

title: Dupahiya — Season 2
description: Dhadakpur remains lovable, but its problems are multiplying faster than its ideas.
review: Returning to Dhadakpur feels like meeting relatives who begin arguing before you have even sat down. That familiarity is the main attraction of Dupahiya's second season.

A mobile tower becomes the latest source of village confusion, while Roshni's examination and Bhugol's changing ambitions introduce more personal concerns. The show understands how one small issue can become everybody's business.
Gajraj Rao, Renuka Shahane and Sparsh Shrivastava help the village feel inhabited rather than assembled for jokes. The humour works best when characters behave according to their own peculiar logic.
The weakness is overcrowding. A mobile tower, a government examination, social-media fame and local politics all compete for attention. Not every detour earns its place.
The first season benefited from the freshness of discovering this world. Season two must work harder because the audience already understands the village's comic rhythm.
It is pleasant company rather than essential television. The cast makes Dhadakpur worth revisiting, even when the writing forgets which road it is travelling on.
works: Familiar characters, warm rural humour, ensemble performances and gentle social satire.
misses: Too many subplots, reduced novelty and inconsistent narrative focus.

title: #Love
description: Two people build dating algorithms, then discover that attraction refuses to follow instructions.
review: There is a funny contradiction at the centre of #Love. Tara and Matthew believe they can explain romance through competing apps, yet their own behaviour keeps challenging those explanations.
Aishwarya Lekshmi brings confidence and vulnerability to Tara. Arjun Das gives Matthew a relaxed charm. Their conversations are more convincing than the corporate competition surrounding them.

The 60-day challenge offers an entertaining structure, but the series does not explore the dating technology as deeply as it could. Algorithms become a convenient argument rather than a fully developed part of the world.

The more important question is whether compatibility and chemistry are really enemies. A lasting relationship probably needs both, along with the willingness to change when another person's needs become inconvenient.
Some emotional conversations end just as they begin to reveal something difficult. The writing seems reluctant to let the couple remain uncomfortable for long.
The leads make this a pleasant watch. But the series talks about understanding love more confidently than it understands its own characters.
works: Aishwarya Lekshmi and Arjun Das, natural chemistry, modern dating premise and light humour.
misses: Underdeveloped technology, simplified emotional conflicts and predictable romantic turns.

title: Mother Promise
description: A Kannada gangster comedy where nonsense eventually finds a surprisingly human purpose.
review: Mother Promise seems determined to make normal behaviour impossible. Characters carry bizarre nicknames, problems multiply and a missing bag becomes an excuse for a parade of comic encounters.

The important thing about absurd comedy is confidence. If a film keeps apologizing for being ridiculous, the audience stops believing in its world. Director Poornachandra Mysore appears comfortable with the madness.
Dhananjaya and the ensemble give the material energy. Navaneeth Sham's music adds another layer of personality to a film that rarely wants to sit quietly.
Not every joke will land. Viewers who need sensible decisions and tidy plotting may find the constant chaos exhausting. But absurdity can have its own rhythm when the performers commit to it.
The emotional thread matters because laughter alone is not always enough to make a film memorable. The idea of a mother's promise gives the comedy somewhere to arrive.
This is not polished, restrained cinema. It is a film that wants the audience to surrender to its eccentricity, and there is value in that confidence.
works: Fearless absurd humour, energetic ensemble, music and an emotional idea beneath the chaos.
misses: Uneven jokes, deliberately exaggerated situations and limited appeal for realism-minded viewers.

title: Carrie — Season 1
description: A familiar horror tragedy enters the age of social media, where humiliation never stays private.
review: The frightening thing about Carrie has never been her supernatural power alone. It is the ordinary cruelty that makes that power dangerous.
Mike Flanagan brings the story into a world where bullying can follow a teenager home through a screen. Public humiliation becomes permanent, searchable and shareable.

Summer H. Howell gives Carrie vulnerability, while Samantha Sloyan's Margaret remains central to the suffocating family relationship. The horror grows from the distance between protection and control.
An eight-episode format creates room for more characters and competing perspectives. That expansion is interesting, but it also changes the concentration of the original tragedy.

The series becomes less morally uncomfortable when it shifts responsibility away from Carrie. A story about a victim who can also become dangerous is more challenging than a story that explains away every terrible choice.
There are strong performances and compelling modern ideas here. The reservation is that greater compassion sometimes comes at the cost of sharper horror.
Carrie remains worth watching because its question is still relevant: how much cruelty does a community excuse before it finally recognizes what it has created?
works: Summer H. Howell, Samantha Sloyan, modern bullying themes and character-focused horror.
misses: Expanded subplots, reduced moral ambiguity and uneven tension across eight episodes.
